ask.changes_what: Positive items push the Wells score toward moderate/high: order compression ultrasound (or CTPA) rather than relying on D-dimer alone; negative items lower the score and enable D-dimer exclusion.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use individual risk factors alone to exclude VTE; do not apply Wells-based D-dimer exclusion to inpatients, pregnant patients, or those already anticoagulated, where the derivation cohorts do not apply.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypotension, syncope or hypoxia with any VTE risk factor mandates immediate imaging or empiric anticoagulation, not D-dimer triage.

ask.how: Ask directly: bed rest >=3 days or major surgery within the past 4-12 weeks; any previous DVT or PE confirmed by imaging; cancer treated within 6 months or palliative. Record each item separately for the Wells DVT or PE score rather than as a global impression.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of individual risk factors does not exclude VTE; a low Wells score (LR ~0.25) plus a negative D-dimer is what allows exclusion without imaging.
ask.pitfalls: Risk-factor LRs were pooled from heterogeneous cohorts and are weaker in patients with prior VTE. Malignancy and prior VTE also raise D-dimer, so they do not license D-dimer-only exclusion in high-probability patients.
ask.positive_finding: Any single risk factor raises the probability of DVT only modestly (pooled LR+ about 1.8-2.7); the value comes from combining items in a Wells score, where a high score carries LR ~5.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or collateral historian able to give a reliable history; check the chart for prior imaging-confirmed VTE and oncology history.
ask.rationale: Knowing VTE risk factors directly impacts the likelihood of PE and guides the need for imaging versus D-dimer.
ask.title: VTE risk history (Wells items): immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4-12 weeks, prior objectively confirmed VTE, active malignancy

ask.changes_what: Shaking chills should prompt blood cultures and a search for a bacteremic source (line, biliary, urinary, endovascular); no chills supports withholding cultures when pretest probability is low.
ask.do_not_use_when: The RCE conclusions do not apply to immunocompromised patients or when endocarditis is suspected; in those groups obtain cultures regardless of chills.
ask.escalation_warning: Rigors with hypotension, altered mentation or a central line indicate probable bacteremia/sepsis: cultures, source control and antibiotics within the hour.

evidence.citation: Coburn B, Morris AM, Tomlinson G, Detsky AS. Does this adult patient with suspected bacteremia require blood cultures? JAMA. 2012;308(5):502-511.
evidence.population: Adult immunocompetent patients in whom bacteremia was suspected (35 studies; 4566 bacteremia and 25,946 negative episodes)
evidence.quote: The severity of chills graded on an ordinal scale (shaking chills, LR, 4.7; 95% CI, 3.0-7.2) may be more useful.
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia (true-positive blood culture)

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: Shaking chills showed a specificity of 90.3% (95% CI 89.2-91.5) and positive likelihood ratio of 4.65 (95% CI 2.95-6.86).
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: shaking chills (whole-body shaking under a thick blanket)

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: The absence of chills showed a sensitivity of 87.5% (95% CI 74.4-94.5) and negative likelihood ratio of 0.24 (95% CI 0.11-0.51).
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: any chills (sensitivity and LR- refer to absence of chills)

ask.how: Ask the patient (or witnesses) whether they have had chills and grade the worst episode: mild = feeling cold, needing a jacket; moderate = needing a thick blanket; shaking chills = whole-body shaking even under a thick blanket. Record timing relative to fever and any line, procedure or infusion.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of any chills lowers the probability of bacteremia (LR- 0.24) but does not exclude it, particularly in elderly or immunocompromised patients who may not mount rigors.
ask.pitfalls: Rigors also occur with malaria, transfusion or drug reactions, and after amphotericin or contaminated infusions; the grading relies on patient recall and the RCE data exclude immunocompromised patients and suspected endocarditis.
ask.positive_finding: Shaking (rigor-grade) chills raise the probability of bacteremia about 4.7-fold (LR+ 4.7, 95% CI 3.0-7.2; specificity 0.90) and justify blood cultures before antibiotics.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or witness able to describe the episode; ask before antipyretics blunt recall.
ask.rationale: Rigors suggest bacteremia and help prioritize pneumonia or sepsis as a cause of fever and chest pain.
ask.title: Rigors / shaking chills

ask.changes_what: Positive: escalate to ADD-RS assessment, CXR/D-dimer and CT angiography as appropriate; negative onset lowers but does not eliminate dissection probability.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use gradual onset alone to exclude dissection in patients with other high-risk features (Marfan/aortic disease, pulse deficit, neurologic deficit, new murmur, hypotension).
ask.escalation_warning: Abrupt severe chest/back pain with hypotension, pulse deficit, or neurologic deficit is a dissection or ruptured AAA until proven otherwise: immediate CT angiography and surgical notification.

evidence.citation: Klompas M. Does this patient have an acute thoracic aortic dissection? JAMA. 2002;287(17):2262-2272.
evidence.population: Consecutive patients with confirmed thoracic aortic dissection from 21 studies (case series; sensitivity pooled; LR- derived from comparison cohorts)
evidence.quote: sudden onset (sensitivity, 84%). The absence of sudden pain onset lowers the likelihood of dissection (negative likelihood ratio [LR], 0.3; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.2-0.5)
evidence.reference_standard: Dissection confirmed by imaging, surgery, or autopsy
evidence.target_condition: Acute thoracic aortic dissection (finding: sudden-onset pain)

evidence.citation: Ohle R, Um J, Anjum O, et al. High risk clinical features for acute aortic dissection: a case-control study. Acad Emerg Med. 2018;25(4):378-384.
evidence.population: Matched case-control: 194 ED/in-hospital CT- or echo-confirmed AAD cases vs 776 ED controls with truncal pain <14 days and no clear diagnosis
evidence.quote: Absence of abrupt-onset pain (sensitivity = 95.9%, negative likelihood ratio = 0.07 [0.03-0.14]) can help rule out AAD.
evidence.reference_standard: CT angiography or echocardiography confirmed dissection
evidence.target_condition: Acute aortic dissection (finding: abrupt-onset pain)

ask.how: Ask an open question about how the pain began, then specifically: 'Did it reach its worst within seconds, or build up over minutes?' Document time-to-peak intensity and whether the patient can pinpoint the moment of onset (what they were doing). Also ask about tearing/ripping quality and migration.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of sudden onset lowers the likelihood of dissection (LR- 0.3 in the RCE pooled series; 0.07 in an ED case-control study), but the clinical examination is insufficiently sensitive to rule out dissection on its own.
ask.pitfalls: Patients recall onset imprecisely, particularly after analgesia or when pain was preceded by exertion; gradual-onset presentations still occur in ~5-16% of dissections, especially in elderly patients or with painless neurologic presentations.
ask.positive_finding: Abrupt-onset pain is present in ~84-96% of aortic dissections but is common in other conditions, so it raises suspicion for dissection only modestly (specificity not established in unselected cohorts); it is a high-risk feature in the ADD risk score.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give history; otherwise ask witnesses or EMS about onset.
ask.rationale: Abrupt, maximal onset pain raises suspicion for aortic dissection, which must not be missed in acute chest pain.
ask.title: Pain abrupt in onset and maximal at onset (thunderclap-type chest/back pain)

examine.changes_what: Unilateral absence after chest trauma or with hypotension: treat as pneumothorax/hemothorax until imaged (POCUS/CXR); with dullness, evaluate for effusion or consolidation.
examine.contraindications: None; do not delay decompression of a clinically obvious tension pneumothorax to complete the exam.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on auscultation alone to exclude pneumothorax in an unstable trauma patient or before positive-pressure ventilation; use POCUS or CXR.
examine.escalation_warning: Unilateral absent breath sounds with hypotension, distended neck veins or tracheal deviation is tension physiology: decompress immediately, do not wait for imaging.

evidence.citation: Arts L, Lim EHT, van de Ven PM, Heunks L, Tuinman PR. The diagnostic accuracy of lung auscultation in adult patients with acute pulmonary pathologies: a meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2020;10:7347.
evidence.location: Table 3, row 'Abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds - (Hemato) pneumothorax'
evidence.population: Adults with blunt or penetrating chest trauma (5 studies; abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds)
evidence.target_condition: Hemothorax, pneumothorax or hematopneumothorax

evidence.citation: Arts L, Lim EHT, van de Ven PM, Heunks L, Tuinman PR. The diagnostic accuracy of lung auscultation in adult patients with acute pulmonary pathologies: a meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2020;10:7347.

evidence.population: Adults with acute respiratory symptoms or suspected pneumonia (6 studies; abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds)
evidence.target_condition: Pneumonia

examine.how: Auscultate both hemithoraces at matched anterior, lateral and posterior points during quiet then deep breathing, comparing each site directly with its mirror-image contralateral site. Note whether breath sounds are absent, markedly reduced or merely asymmetric, and check tracheal position in the suprasternal notch.
examine.negative_finding: Symmetric, normal-intensity vesicular breath sounds bilaterally; this lowers but does not exclude small pneumothorax, effusion or pneumonia.
examine.pitfalls: Sounds transmit across the mediastinum and the finding is insensitive (pooled sensitivity around 0.5-0.7), so a normal exam cannot rule out pneumothorax. Obesity, COPD hyperinflation, shallow breathing and noisy resuscitation bays reduce reliability.
examine.positive_finding: Breath sounds clearly absent or much reduced on one side compared with the other, with or without hyperresonance (pneumothorax) or dullness (effusion/consolidation).
examine.prerequisites: Quiet room, skin contact (not through clothing), patient able to breathe on request; in trauma, examine during primary survey with the patient supine.
examine.rationale: Unilateral absent breath sounds would rapidly prioritize pneumothorax, a treatable emergency.
examine.title: Unilaterally absent or markedly reduced breath sounds (+/- tracheal deviation as late tension sign)

examine.changes_what: RR >24 with fever/cough: image for pneumonia and assess severity. Normal vitals in low-risk cough: CXR may be deferred. Unexplained tachypnea: check gas/lactate for acidosis.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal RR to exclude PE, sepsis or acidosis; do not rely on charted (estimated) rates.
examine.escalation_warning: RR >=30, or RR >=22 with altered mentation or SBP <=100 (qSOFA >=2), or tachypnea with rising PCO2/fatigue: escalate to higher level of care.

evidence.citation: Htun TP, Sun Y, Chua HL, Pang J. Clinical features for diagnosis of pneumonia among adults in primary care setting: A systematic and meta-review. Sci Rep. 2019;9:7600.
evidence.location: Table 2 (PMC6527561 full text); footnote ¥ gives thresholds
evidence.population: Adults with respiratory symptoms in primary care, no serious illness; 6 studies, n=4,468
evidence.target_condition: Radiographic community-acquired pneumonia (respiratory rate >=20/min; >=22 in one study, >=24 in two)

evidence.citation: Ebell MH, Chupp H, Cai X, Bentivegna M, Kearney M. Accuracy of Signs and Symptoms for the Diagnosis of Community-acquired Pneumonia: A Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(7):541-553.
evidence.population: Adults with suspected pneumonia or acute cough; 17 prospective cohorts (9 primary care, 7 ED)
evidence.quote: it is decreased most by the absence of abnormal vital signs (LR- = 0.25, 95% CI = 0.11 to 0.48)
evidence.target_condition: Community-acquired pneumonia (absence of ANY abnormal vital sign, composite including respiratory rate)

examine.how: Count chest-wall excursions for a full 60 seconds while the patient is at rest and unaware (e.g., while appearing to take the pulse). Do not use the triage estimate or a 15-second count multiplied; record the pattern (deep Kussmaul vs shallow rapid) as well as the rate.
examine.negative_finding: A normal rate lowers but does not exclude pneumonia (LR- 0.77); absence of any vital-sign abnormality lowers CAP probability more strongly (LR- 0.25).
examine.pitfalls: Recorded rates are often estimated rather than counted, clustering at 18-20. Pain, anxiety, fever and hypoxia raise the rate nonspecifically; PE frequently presents with RR >20 but the finding is not discriminating.
examine.positive_finding: RR above threshold raises the probability of radiographic pneumonia (pooled LR+ 3.5 for RR >=20-24) and is a qSOFA/CURB-65 criterion; deep regular tachypnea points to metabolic acidosis or uremia.
examine.prerequisites: Patient at rest for several minutes; not talking.
examine.rationale: Tachypnea is a key severity marker and may indicate PE, pneumonia, or other acute processes.
examine.title: Respiratory rate >24-25/min counted for 60 s

examine.changes_what: Bilateral: pursue spirometry/COPD; unilateral with breath-sound loss: obtain CXR or POCUS for pneumothorax now; normal: no change in probability.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid delaying decompression for percussion in a hypotensive patient with suspected tension pneumothorax.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use percussion to exclude pneumothorax in trauma or after a procedure; image instead.
examine.escalation_warning: Unilateral hyperresonance with absent breath sounds, hypotension or tracheal deviation = tension pneumothorax; decompress before imaging.

evidence.citation: Oshaug K, Halvorsen PA, Melbye H. Should chest examination be reinstated in the early diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease? Int J Chron Obstruct Pulmon Dis. 2013.
evidence.population: 375 primary-care patients aged >=40 y with a previous diagnosis of asthma or COPD (cross-sectional, Norway)
evidence.quote: Hyperresonance to percussion  0.21  0.98  9.5  3.7-23.7  86.1
evidence.target_condition: COPD (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7)

evidence.citation: Oshaug K, Halvorsen PA, Melbye H. Should chest examination be reinstated in the early diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease? Int J Chron Obstruct Pulmon Dis. 2013.
evidence.population: Same 375 primary-care patients aged >=40 y with previous asthma/COPD diagnosis
evidence.quote: Hyperresonance to percussion  0.39  0.94  6.7  3.8-12.0  47.2
evidence.reference_standard: Post-bronchodilator spirometry (severe COPD definition per Table 4)
evidence.target_condition: Severe COPD (post-bronchodilator spirometry threshold as defined in Table 4)

examine.how: With the patient sitting, percuss symmetric points over both lung fields anteriorly and posteriorly, comparing side to side; hyperresonance is a louder, lower-pitched, more drum-like note than normal resonance. Note whether it is bilateral (hyperinflation) or unilateral (air in the pleural space), and combine with breath-sound asymmetry.
examine.negative_finding: Normal percussion note does not exclude COPD (sensitivity about 0.2) or a small pneumothorax; the sign is a rule-in, not a rule-out, finding.
examine.pitfalls: Obesity, a thick chest wall and examiner skill blunt the sign; interobserver agreement for percussion is poor. Large bullae or a contralateral effusion can mimic unilateral hyperresonance.
examine.positive_finding: Bilateral hyperresonance in a smoker strongly raises the probability of COPD (LR+ about 9.5 in primary care); unilateral hyperresonance with reduced breath sounds points to pneumothorax on that side.
examine.prerequisites: Quiet room, chest exposed, examiner able to compare with normal resonance.
examine.rationale: Hyperresonance on percussion can quickly point to pneumothorax, especially with sudden pleuritic pain.
examine.title: Chest percussion hyperresonance (diffuse with barrel chest = COPD; unilateral = pneumothorax)

examine.changes_what: Loud P2 or RV heave: move to echocardiography for RV pressure and function. Absent signs should not lower suspicion of PH or PE when the history is suggestive.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on these signs to exclude PH, RV failure or PE; do not use them to defer echo in a hypotensive or syncopal patient.
examine.escalation_warning: RV heave or loud P2 with hypotension, syncope, or rising JVP suggests acute RV failure (massive PE, PH crisis) and needs immediate echo and escalation.

evidence.quote: a loud P2 on inspiration (specificity 87%, sensitivity 37%, positive LR 3.2, 95% CrI [1.5, 6.2])

examine.how: Patient supine at 30-45 degrees. Place the heel of the hand over the left lower sternal border and feel for a sustained outward lift during systole (RV heave), then palpate the 2nd left interspace for a palpable P2. Auscultate the pulmonic area for a loud pulmonic component of S2, comparing intensity with A2, at rest and during a slow inspiration.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of either sign does not exclude pulmonary hypertension; all negative LRs were about 0.7-1.0 and no finding reliably ruled PH out.
examine.pitfalls: Sensitivity is low (21-43%) and generalist examiners performed no better than chance for these signs. A parasternal lift can also come from left atrial enlargement in mitral regurgitation or from a thin chest wall.
examine.positive_finding: A loud P2 modestly raises the probability of pulmonary hypertension (mPAP >=25 mmHg): LR+ 1.6 at rest and 1.9 on inspiration for all examiners, 3.2 when elicited by a specialist. An RV lift has LR+ about 1.1-1.3 and is essentially non-discriminating.
examine.prerequisites: Quiet room; patient not in acute respiratory distress that prevents breath control.
examine.rationale: A parasternal heave or loud P[n] suggests acute right heart strain, supporting PE as a leading diagnosis.
examine.title: Left parasternal (RV) heave and loud/palpable P2
